'''''Ficus subpisocarpa''''', commonly known as '''Japanese superb fig''', '''superb fig''' or '''pen tube fig''',<ref name="Zhang2023">{{Cite book |last=Zhang |first=Allen |title=香港100種景觀樹木圖鑑 |publisher=萬里機構 |year=2023 |isbn=9789621474872 |location=Hong Kong |pages=69-71 |language=zh-hant, en |trans-title=A Photographic Guide to 100 Ornamental Trees of Hong Kong}}</ref> is a species of [[Ficus|fig]] native to Japan, China, Hong Kong,<ref name="Zhang2023" /> Taiwan and southeast Asia to the [[Moluccas]] (Ceram).<ref name=bergcorner05>{{cite book|author1=Berg, C.C.  |author2=Corner E.J.H.|year=2005| title= Flora Malesiana |chapter=Moraceae|series=I|volume=17|issue=6| isbn= 1-930723-40-7}}</ref> Terrestrial or hemiepiphytic, it reaches a height of {{convert|12|m|ft|abbr=on}}. Ants, predominantly of the genus ''[[Crematogaster]]'', have been recorded living in stem cavities.

==Taxonomy==
''Ficus subpisocarpa'' was described by the French botanist [[François Gagnepain]] in 1927, from a collection near Haiphong in Vietnam. It was reduced to a synonym of ''F. superba'' variety ''japonica'' by [[E. J. H. Corner]] in 1965,<ref name=Corner-1965>{{Cite journal | last1= Corner | first1= E. J. H. | author-link1= E. J. H. Corner | year= 1965 | title= Check-list of ''Ficus'' in Asia and Australasia with keys to identification | journal= The Gardens' Bulletin Singapore | volume= 21 | issue= 1 | pages= 1–186 | url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/43581709 | version= (digitised, online, via biodiversitylibrary.org) | access-date= 5 Feb 2014 }}</ref> before being raised to species status again by [[Cornelis Christiaan Berg]] in 2005.<ref name=berg07>{{cite journal|author=Berg, Cornelis C. |year=2007 |title=Precursory taxonomic studies on ''Ficus'' (Moraceae) for the Flora of Thailand |journal=Thai Forest Bulletin. Botany |volume=35 |pages=4–28 |url=http://web3.dnp.go.th/botany/PDF/TFB/TFB35/TFB35_2Ficus.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140221225358/http://web3.dnp.go.th/botany/PDF/TFB/TFB35/TFB35_2Ficus.pdf |archive-date=2014-02-21 }}</ref> Within the genus, ''Ficus subpisocarpa'' belongs in the banyan subgenus ''Urostigma'' section ''Urostigma'' subsection ''Urostigma''.<ref name=berg07/> Two subspecies are recognised:<ref name="POWO"/>
*''Ficus subpisocarpa'' subsp. ''subpisocarpa'' – petiole glabrous.<ref name=berg07/>
*''Ficus subpisocarpa'' subsp. ''pubipoda'' C.C.Berg – distinguished by having the base of the petiole puberulent, with short white hairs.<ref name=berg07/>

==Description==
''Ficus subpisocarpa'' is a tree that grows up to {{convert|12|m|ft|abbr=off}} high,<ref name="Taiwan">{{cite journal | last1=Chiang | first1=Yun-Peng | last2=Bain | first2=Anthony | last3=Wu | first3=Wen-Jer | last4=Chou | first4=Lien-Siang | title=Adaptive phenology of Ficus subpisocarpa and Ficus caulocarpa in Taipei, Taiwan | journal=Acta Oecologica | volume=90 | date=2018 | doi=10.1016/j.actao.2017.11.013 | pages=35–45 | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1146609X1630368X | access-date=2025-08-26| url-access=subscription }}</ref> growing from the ground or directly on other trees as a [[hemiepiphyte]]. The bark is dark brown,<ref name=FoC/> while the branches are reddish brown to dark grey.<ref name=berg07/> The foliage is deciduous in at least some areas,<ref name=FoC/> but possibly not in other areas,<ref name=berg07/><ref name="FM">{{cite web | title=''Ficus subpisocarpa'' | website=Flora Malesiana | url=https://portal.cybertaxonomy.org/flora-malesiana/cdm_dataportal/taxon/6a7c4268-35f8-4876-b476-fa703a15624c | access-date=2025-08-26}}</ref> and trees may only be leafless for a week before new leaves grow.<ref name="Taiwan"/> The leaves and [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]s are [[glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]] (hairless), and the leaves are symmetrical, elliptical and oblong with a rounded base, and can measure anywhere from {{convert|4|to|24|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|1.5|–|13|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide. They are [[phyllotaxis|spirally arranged]] on the stem.<ref name=berg07/> The growth of new tissue occurs when a whole section of the branch undergoes budding and becomes covered with leaves. The figs are [[Ramiflory|ramiflorous]], that is they grow on the branches, in groups of one to three.<ref name=berg07/> There is a high variation in colour between trees and seasons; mature figs are whitish pink to dark purple, often patterned with pale spots, are bulbous to globose, and measure {{convert|0.5|to|0.8|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name="Borneo">{{cite web | title=Ficus subpisocarpa: Introduction | website=The Figs of Borneo | date=2023-12-10 | url=https://borneoficus.info/2023/12/10/ficus-subpisocarpa-introduction/ | access-date=2025-08-26}}</ref><ref name=berg07/><ref name=FoC/> Maturation is also highly variable, even on a single tree; it is synchronous up until the pollinating [[fig wasp]]s emerge, but variable after that, with some figs maturing rapidly but others only fully ripe five weeks after wasp emergence.<ref name="Taiwan"/> Two to four crops of figs can be produced in a year.<ref name=bain12/> ''Ficus subpisocarpa'' is pollinated by fig wasps in the genus ''[[Platyscapa]]'' ([[Agaonidae]]),<ref name="Taiwan"/> specifically ''P. ishiiana''.{{CN|date=August 2025}}

==Distribution and habitat==
The nominate subspecies is found from Southern Japan, Taiwan, Hainan and eastern China (where it occurs in Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, southern Yunnan and southeastern Zhejiang provinces), through Vietnam, Laos and Thailand into Indonesia where it reaches Ceram in the Moluccas. It is possibly found in Cambodia.<ref name=berg07/><ref name=FoC>{{cite book|author1=Wu, Z. |author2=Raven, P.H. |author3=Hong, D. |year=2003|title= Flora of China. Volume 5: Ulmaceae through Basellaceae |location= Beijing and St Louis|publisher= Missouri Botanical Garden Press | isbn= 1-930723-40-7 |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242414769 |page=40}}</ref> Subspecies ''pubipoda'' is found in Vietnam, Cambodia, Thailand and Peninsular Malaysia.<ref name=berg07/>

Both subspecies are found in deciduous and evergreen forests, the nominate at low elevations and subspecies ''pubipoda'' to {{convert|1400|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref name=berg07/>

==Ecology==
In a field study in Taiwan, ants were found to inhabit cavities within internodes of young branches of ''Ficus subpisocarpa''.<ref name=bain12/> They feed on wasps, more commonly on non-pollinating rather than the pollinating species necessary for the fig to reproduce. It is possible that the fig developed the cavities to accommodate the ants. 75% of ants recorded in the study belonged to the genus ''[[Crematogaster]]'', with the remainder belonging to the genera ''[[Technomyrmex]]'', ''[[Myrmica]]'' and ''[[Prenolepis]]''. Sometimes two ant species shared the cavities. The cavities mostly ranged between {{convert|2|and|14|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in length. The ants appear to tend aphids and scale insects that are present on the fig plant.<ref name=bain12>{{cite journal|author=Bain, A.|author2=Chantarasuwan, B.|author3=Hossaert-McKey, M.|author4=Schatz, B.|author5=Kjellberg, F.|author6=Chou, L.-S.|name-list-style=amp|year=2012|title= A new case of ants nesting within branches of a fig tree: the case of ''Ficus subpisocarpa'' in Taiwan|journal= Sociobiology |volume= 59|issue=1|pages= 415–34|doi=10.13102/sociobiology.v59i2.604|doi-access=free}}</ref>
''Ficus subpisocarpa'' is the second ''Ficus'' species observed with ants inhabiting branch cavities, the first observation was done in Borneo on ''Ficus obscura'' var. ''borneensis''.<ref name=Maschwitz94>{{cite journal|author=Maschwitz, U.|author2=Fiala, B.|author3=Saw, L.G.|author4=Yusoff, N.-R.|author5=Idris, A.H.|name-list-style=amp|year=1994|title= ''Ficus obscura'' var. ''borneensis'' (Moraceae), a new non-specific ant-plant from Malesia |journal= Malayan Nature Journal |volume= 47|pages= 409–16}}</ref>
{{Clear|left}}

== Uses ==
The rigidity of its bark makes it suitable for carving and sculpture. The species also develops a broad crown that provides ample shade, and it is therefore widely planted along streets and in parks.<ref name="Zhang2023" />
